# IV audit checklist (v0.15, generated by scripts/skillgen)

13 checks. Each rests on claims from the methods literature, and each one points to where to read more. The 15 sources listed under **Sources** below are the ones cited in the further-reading lines.

**How to read a verdict.** `PASS` / `FLAG` are decided by the stated conditions. `NA` means the check is out of scope for this design — never that the paper was silent. When a check applies and the paper says nothing, the verdict is the one given in *When silent*.

**Evidence scope.** A verdict covers only the text the audit could see. A FLAG on material the paper says is in an appendix or replication package means "not shown here", not "not done" — such flags carry that caveat in the report.

**Thresholds are rules of thumb unless marked otherwise.** Where a cutoff is conventional rather than derived, the item says so, and near-threshold values are reported as borderline rather than silently rounded to a verdict.

## Scope triggers

A check applies only when its scope trigger fires. Triggers key on the paper's own explicit stance and default OUT when the paper is silent.

- **`all`** — The paper states it estimates a causal effect of an endogenous regressor using an instrumental variable (2SLS/IV/GMM with an excluded instrument). Fires on any paper that names an instrument for an endogenous regressor. A paper that runs only OLS/regression adjustment and never names an instrument is out of scope.
- **`as_if_random_or_conditional`** — Fires when the paper describes its instrument as randomly or as-if-randomly assigned (lottery/natural experiment), or as valid only conditional on named covariates. Near-miss that does NOT fire: an instrument defended purely by theoretical argument with no claim of (conditional) random assignment.
- **`late_causal`** — The paper states it interprets its IV estimate as an average causal/treatment effect: it invokes potential outcomes or compliers/LATE, or it explicitly allows the treatment effect to vary across units (heterogeneous effects) and reads the 2SLS coefficient as such an average. Fires only on an explicit causal-effect reading. NEAR-MISS that does NOT fire: a paper that explicitly assumes a single constant/homogeneous structural coefficient and reports only that slope, making no complier/average-treatment-effect claim; a purely predictive/first-stage-only exercise. Ambiguity resolves OUT (NA): a coder never infers a causal-effect reading, or effect heterogeneity, the paper did not state.
- **`multiple_endogenous`** — The paper states it instruments two or more endogenous regressors jointly in the same equation. Fires on a declared count >1 of endogenous regressors. NEAR-MISS: a single endogenous regressor with several instruments (overidentified but one endogenous variable) does NOT fire.

## IDENT

*Identification — the assumptions the causal claim rests on.*

### IV-IDENT-01 — State the target causal parameter the IV estimate is meant to identify.

**Scope:** `all` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** HIGH (3 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** The paper should state in words which causal effect its instrumental variable (IV) estimate is meant to capture and, if that effect applies only to a particular group, name that group.

**Why it matters:** Without a stated target, readers cannot tell what quantity the estimate represents or whom it describes.

**Check:** Whether the paper contains an explicit statement naming the causal parameter being estimated (e.g., the effect of the endogenous regressor on the outcome for a named population).

- **Pass:** The paper names, in words, the causal parameter it estimates; where that parameter is population-specific (e.g., a local effect), it also identifies the population it applies to.
- **Flag:** The paper reports an IV estimate without ever stating which causal parameter it is meant to identify.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Thad Dunning. (2012). Natural Experiments in the Social Sciences. Cambridge University Press eBooks. https://doi.org/10.1017/cbo9781139084444 — p. 33
  - Andrew Gelman & Jennifer Hill. (2006). Data Analysis Using Regression and Multilevel/Hierarchical Models. Cambridge University Press eBooks. https://doi.org/10.1017/cbo9780511790942 — p. 220
  - Allison J. Sovey & Donald P. Green. (2010). Instrumental Variables Estimation in Political Science: A Readers’ Guide. American Journal of Political Science, 55(1), 188-200. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-5907.2010.00477.x — p. 188

### IV-IDENT-02 — Argue, substantively, why the instrument influences the outcome only through the endogenous regressor.

**Scope:** `all` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** HIGH (5 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** The paper should give a reasoned argument, not a statistical test, for why the instrument affects the outcome only through the treatment (the exclusion restriction); a regression of the outcome on the instrument does not count.

**Why it matters:** This assumption cannot be tested with the data, so the estimate is only as credible as the argument for it.

**Check:** Whether the paper presents reasoning (not a statistical test) defending that the instrument has no pathway to the outcome except through the treatment.

- **Pass:** The paper gives an explicit substantive argument for the exclusion restriction, findable anywhere in the paper or its appendices.
- **Flag:** The paper invokes an instrument but offers no argued defense of the exclusion restriction, or defends it only by an OLS regression of the outcome on the instrument.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Timothy G. Conley, Christian Hansen, & Peter E. Rossi. (2010). Plausibly Exogenous. The Review of Economics and Statistics, 94(1), 260-272. https://doi.org/10.1162/rest_a_00139 — p. 260
  - Hans van Kippersluis & Cornelius A. Rietveld. (2018). Beyond plausibly exogenous. Econometrics Journal, 21(3), 316-331. https://doi.org/10.1111/ectj.12113 — p. 316
  - Edward Miguel, Shanker Satyanath, & Ernest Sergenti. (2004). Economic Shocks and Civil Conflict: An Instrumental Variables Approach. Journal of Political Economy, 112(4), 725-753. https://doi.org/10.1086/421174 — p. 745
  - Allison J. Sovey & Donald P. Green. (2010). Instrumental Variables Estimation in Political Science: A Readers’ Guide. American Journal of Political Science, 55(1), 188-200. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-5907.2010.00477.x — p. 190

### IV-IDENT-03 — The paper must argue the instrument is (as-if) independent of the outcome's unobserved determinants, explicitly when it is not physically randomized.

**Scope:** `all` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** HIGH (7 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** The paper should argue that the instrument is unrelated to hidden factors that affect the outcome, as if randomly assigned, making this case explicitly when it was not actually randomized and naming any covariates it conditions on.

**Why it matters:** IV relies on this independence, and outside a true randomization it cannot simply be assumed.

**Check:** Whether the paper argues that the instrument is unrelated to outcome confounders / as-good-as-randomly assigned, and (when not physically randomized) makes that case rather than assuming it.

- **Pass:** The paper argues the instrument is independent of confounders of the treatment-outcome relationship, e.g. by establishing (conditional) random or as-if-random assignment and naming the conditioning covariates it relies on.
- **Flag:** The paper treats a non-randomized instrument as exogenous without argument, or rests independence on an a-priori belief with no supporting reasoning.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Joshua D. Angrist, Guido W. Imbens, & Donald B. Rubin. (1996). Identification of Causal Effects Using Instrumental Variables. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 91(434), 444-455. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1996.10476902 — p. 450
  - Thad Dunning. (2012). Natural Experiments in the Social Sciences. Cambridge University Press eBooks. https://doi.org/10.1017/cbo9781139084444 — p. 28
  - Andrew Gelman & Jennifer Hill. (2006). Data Analysis Using Regression and Multilevel/Hierarchical Models. Cambridge University Press eBooks. https://doi.org/10.1017/cbo9780511790942 — p. 225
  - Hans van Kippersluis & Cornelius A. Rietveld. (2018). Beyond plausibly exogenous. Econometrics Journal, 21(3), 316-331. https://doi.org/10.1111/ectj.12113 — p. 318

### IV-IDENT-04 — A paper claiming (conditional) random assignment must report a balance/randomization check of the instrument against predetermined covariates.

**Scope:** `as_if_random_or_conditional` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** HIGH (4 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** If the paper claims the instrument is (conditionally) randomly assigned, it should check that the instrument is unrelated to characteristics fixed before assignment, using the same covariates as in its estimates.

**Why it matters:** Random assignment implies the instrument should be unrelated to such characteristics, so this check tests the claim directly.

**Check:** Whether the paper reports comparing the instrument against variables fixed before assignment (a balance / randomization check), using the same covariate scheme it uses in estimation.

- **Pass:** The paper reports a balance/randomization check — e.g. tests or comparisons of predetermined covariates across instrument values, or an F-test for unexpected instrument-covariate correlations.
- **Flag:** The paper claims (conditional) random or as-if-random assignment but reports no check of the instrument against predetermined covariates.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Thad Dunning. (2012). Natural Experiments in the Social Sciences. Cambridge University Press eBooks. https://doi.org/10.1017/cbo9781139084444 — p. 11
  - Brigham Frandsen, Lars Lefgren, & Emily Leslie. (2022). Judging Judge Fixed Effects. American Economic Review, 113(1), 253-277. https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.20201860 — p. 259
  - Allison J. Sovey & Donald P. Green. (2010). Instrumental Variables Estimation in Political Science: A Readers’ Guide. American Journal of Political Science, 55(1), 188-200. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-5907.2010.00477.x — p. 198

### IV-IDENT-05 — Justify monotonicity (no defiers) when interpreting the IV estimand as an average treatment effect.

**Scope:** `late_causal` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** HIGH (5 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper reads its IV estimate as an average treatment effect, it should justify, by argument or design, that the instrument pushes no unit's treatment in the opposite direction (no "defiers", also called monotonicity).

**Why it matters:** Without this condition, the IV estimate cannot be read as an average effect when effects may vary across units.

**Check:** Whether the paper states and defends the monotonicity/no-defiers condition (by argument or design).

- **Pass:** A paper with a fired late_causal trigger gives a theoretical or design-based justification that no defiers exist.
- **Flag:** A late_causal paper interprets the IV estimand as an average effect without addressing monotonicity.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Joshua D. Angrist, Guido W. Imbens, & Donald B. Rubin. (1996). Identification of Causal Effects Using Instrumental Variables. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 91(434), 444-455. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1996.10476902 — p. 447
  - Andrew Gelman & Jennifer Hill. (2006). Data Analysis Using Regression and Multilevel/Hierarchical Models. Cambridge University Press eBooks. https://doi.org/10.1017/cbo9780511790942 — p. 217
  - Guido W. Imbens & Joshua D. Angrist. (1994). Identification and Estimation of Local Average Treatment Effects. Econometrica, 62(2), 467. https://doi.org/10.2307/2951620 — p. 469

### IV-IDENT-06 — The paper must address no interference between units (SUTVA), by argument, design, or explicit modeling.

**Scope:** `all` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** HIGH (5 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** The paper should address whether one unit's outcome could be affected by other units' instrument or treatment (interference, or spillovers), either by arguing it does not happen or by modeling it where expected.

**Why it matters:** IV assumes no interference between units, and spillovers between treated and untreated units bias the estimate.

**Check:** Whether the paper addresses no-interference / SUTVA -- by arguing that one unit's outcome is unaffected by other units' assignment or treatment, or by explicitly modeling spillovers where they are expected.

- **Pass:** The paper addresses no interference between units -- arguing from design or context that one unit's outcome is unaffected by other units' assignment/treatment, or explicitly modeling the interference where it is expected.
- **Flag:** The paper neither argues no interference between units nor models spillovers -- it is silent on SUTVA.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Joshua D. Angrist, Guido W. Imbens, & Donald B. Rubin. (1996). Identification of Causal Effects Using Instrumental Variables. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 91(434), 444-455. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1996.10476902 — p. 446
  - Andrew Gelman & Jennifer Hill. (2006). Data Analysis Using Regression and Multilevel/Hierarchical Models. Cambridge University Press eBooks. https://doi.org/10.1017/cbo9780511790942 — p. 216
  - Allison J. Sovey & Donald P. Green. (2010). Instrumental Variables Estimation in Political Science: A Readers’ Guide. American Journal of Political Science, 55(1), 188-200. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-5907.2010.00477.x — p. 197

### IV-IDENT-07 — Acknowledge the local (complier) nature of the IV estimand and its limited generalizability.

**Scope:** `late_causal` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** HIGH (5 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When reading its IV estimate causally, the paper should acknowledge that it applies only to units whose treatment the instrument changes (compliers), not automatically to the whole population.

**Why it matters:** When effects vary across units, the effect for compliers need not equal the population effect, which limits how far the result generalizes.

**Check:** Whether the paper states that its IV estimate applies only to the subpopulation the instrument moves and flags the resulting limit on generalizability.

- **Pass:** A fired late_causal paper states the locality of its estimand (compliers / instrument-shifted range) and does not silently generalize it to the whole population.
- **Flag:** A late_causal paper presents its IV estimate as a population/average effect with no acknowledgment of complier-locality.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Andrew Gelman & Jennifer Hill. (2006). Data Analysis Using Regression and Multilevel/Hierarchical Models. Cambridge University Press eBooks. https://doi.org/10.1017/cbo9780511790942 — p. 219
  - Guido W. Imbens & Joshua D. Angrist. (1994). Identification and Estimation of Local Average Treatment Effects. Econometrica, 62(2), 467. https://doi.org/10.2307/2951620 — p. 470
  - Allison J. Sovey & Donald P. Green. (2010). Instrumental Variables Estimation in Political Science: A Readers’ Guide. American Journal of Political Science, 55(1), 188-200. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-5907.2010.00477.x — p. 193

## INFER

*Inference — standard errors, tests, and their validity.*

### IV-INFER-01 — Report a first-stage instrument-strength statistic (F or partial R-squared of the excluded instruments).

**Scope:** `all` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** HIGH (5 of the module's sources) · **Disputed** — Andrews (2019) argues first-stage F-statistics can be spuriously large even with irrelevant instruments and so may not reliably indicate whether conventional inference performs well, and Olea (2013) argues the ordinary and robust first-stage F cannot substitute for the effective F.

**In plain words:** The paper should report how strongly the instrument predicts the treatment in the first stage, using an F statistic or partial R-squared for the excluded instruments after accounting for covariates.

**Why it matters:** Readers need this statistic to judge whether the instrument is strong enough to support the IV estimate.

**Check:** Whether the paper reports a first-stage strength statistic for the excluded instrument(s).

- **Pass:** The paper reports a first-stage F statistic or partial R-squared of the excluded instruments (partialling out covariates), findable anywhere in the paper or appendices.
- **Flag:** The paper reports IV/2SLS estimates but no first-stage strength statistic.
- **When silent:** FLAG
- **Prevalence:** Surveys find IV papers routinely omit any first-stage relevance statistic (Staiger-Stock 1997; Sovey 2010).

**Further reading**
  - John Bound, David A. Jaeger, & Regina Baker. (1995). Problems with Instrumental Variables Estimation When the Correlation Between the Instruments and the Endogeneous Explanatory Variable is Weak. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 90(430), 443. https://doi.org/10.2307/2291055 — pp. 443-444
  - Douglas O. Staiger & James H. Stock. (1997). Instrumental Variables Regression with Weak Instruments. Econometrica, 65(3), 557. https://doi.org/10.2307/2171753 — p. 582

### IV-INFER-02 — Use identification-robust inference when the first stage is weak.

**Scope:** `all` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** HIGH (5 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** If the instrument is weak or borderline (an effective F below 23.1), the paper should add inference that stays valid with weak instruments, such as an Anderson-Rubin confidence set, rather than relying only on conventional standard errors.

**Why it matters:** With a weak first stage, conventional confidence intervals contain the true value less often than claimed, and rescaling standard errors does not fix this.

**Check:** Whether, given a weak first stage, the paper reports weak-instrument-robust inference rather than relying only on conventional 2SLS standard errors.

- **Pass:** Either the first-stage effective F is at or above the strong-instrument threshold (23.1, the conservative worst-case value for TSLS) and conventional inference is reported; or the effective F is weak/borderline and the paper additionally reports weak-instrument-robust inference (e.g., an Anderson-Rubin confidence set).
- **Flag:** The first-stage effective F is below the strong-instrument threshold and the paper reports only conventional t/Wald standard errors or CIs, with no identification-robust inference.
- **When silent:** FLAG
- **Threshold:** cutoff 10; provenance: rule of thumb; borderline band: [10, 23.1]
- **Inside the band:** Judge strength on the first-stage EFFECTIVE F (not an ordinary F against homoskedastic critical values; see IV-INFER-03). At or above 23.1 (the conservative worst-case effective-F critical value for TSLS) conventional inference alone PASSes; below 10 the first stage is weak and a weak-instrument-robust confidence set is required to PASS; within [10, 23.1] strength is not established at the conservative bound, so PASS only if a weak-instrument-robust confidence set is also reported, otherwise FLAG.

**Further reading**
  - Isaiah Andrews, James H. Stock, & Liyang Sun. (2019). Weak Instruments in Instrumental Variables Regression: Theory and Practice. Annual Review of Economics, 11(1), 727-753. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-economics-080218-025643 — p. 742
  - José Luis Montiel Olea & Carolin Pflueger. (2013). A Robust Test for Weak Instruments. Journal of Business and Economic Statistics, 31(3), 358-369. https://doi.org/10.1080/00401706.2013.806694 — p. 358
  - Douglas O. Staiger & James H. Stock. (1997). Instrumental Variables Regression with Weak Instruments. Econometrica, 65(3), 557. https://doi.org/10.2307/2171753 — p. 565
  - James H. Stock, Jonathan H. Wright, & Motohiro Yogo. (2002). A Survey of Weak Instruments and Weak Identification in Generalized Method of Moments. Journal of Business and Economic Statistics, 20(4), 518-529. https://doi.org/10.1198/073500102288618658 — p. 519

### IV-INFER-03 — Assess instrument strength with an error-structure-matched robust statistic (effective F), not a plain F against homoskedastic critical values.

**Scope:** `all` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** MEDIUM (2 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When errors are clustered, correlated over time, or uneven in spread, the paper should judge instrument strength with a statistic that accounts for this (the effective F), not an ordinary F compared to standard Stock-Yogo cutoffs.

**Why it matters:** Those standard cutoffs assume errors of even spread, so applying them under other error patterns can misjudge whether the instrument is strong enough.

**Check:** Whether the strength diagnostic the paper uses matches its error structure (effective / robust weak-instrument statistic) rather than an ordinary F judged against homoskedastic critical values.

- **Pass:** With non-homoskedastic/clustered/serial errors, the paper assesses strength with a heteroskedasticity/HAC/cluster-robust weak-instrument statistic (e.g., effective F).
- **Flag:** The paper has non-homoskedastic/clustered/serial errors but judges strength by an ordinary (or plain robust) first-stage F against homoskedastic Stock-Yogo values.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Isaiah Andrews, James H. Stock, & Liyang Sun. (2019). Weak Instruments in Instrumental Variables Regression: Theory and Practice. Annual Review of Economics, 11(1), 727-753. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-economics-080218-025643 — pp. 737-738
  - José Luis Montiel Olea & Carolin Pflueger. (2013). A Robust Test for Weak Instruments. Journal of Business and Economic Statistics, 31(3), 358-369. https://doi.org/10.1080/00401706.2013.806694 — p. 365

### IV-INFER-04 — Do not screen/select specifications by a first-stage F threshold.

**Scope:** `all` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** MEDIUM (2 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** The paper should not keep or drop specifications, samples, or instruments based on whether their first-stage F statistic passes a cutoff.

**Why it matters:** Screening on the F statistic biases the estimates that survive and distorts the error rates of the tests.

**Check:** Whether the paper reports keeping/dropping specifications, samples, or instruments on the basis of a first-stage F cutoff.

- **Pass:** The paper does not screen specifications on a first-stage F threshold (silence about such screening passes).
- **Flag:** The paper states it retained only specifications, samples, or instruments whose first-stage F exceeded a cutoff.
- **When silent:** PASS

**Further reading**
  - Isaiah Andrews, James H. Stock, & Liyang Sun. (2019). Weak Instruments in Instrumental Variables Regression: Theory and Practice. Annual Review of Economics, 11(1), 727-753. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-economics-080218-025643 — pp. 740-741

### IV-INFER-05 — Use a variance estimator matched to the error/clustering structure and the two-stage design.

**Scope:** `all` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** HIGH (5 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** The paper should compute standard errors suited to the data's structure, for example clustering at the level where observations are related or correcting for correlation over time, and account for the two estimation stages.

**Why it matters:** Standard errors that ignore this structure or the two-stage estimation can misstate uncertainty, so the reported IV standard errors may not be valid.

**Check:** Whether the reported IV standard errors use a variance estimator appropriate to the design's heteroskedasticity/clustering/serial-correlation and account for the estimation stages.

- **Pass:** The paper reports standard errors from a variance estimator matched to its error structure (e.g., clustered at the dependence level; HAC for time series) and consistent with the two-stage/generated-regressor structure.
- **Flag:** The paper uses default/homoskedastic or mismatched-level standard errors where the design implies clustering or serial correlation, or ignores the two-stage estimation.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Isaiah Andrews, James H. Stock, & Liyang Sun. (2019). Weak Instruments in Instrumental Variables Regression: Theory and Practice. Annual Review of Economics, 11(1), 727-753. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-economics-080218-025643 — p. 732
  - Thad Dunning. (2012). Natural Experiments in the Social Sciences. Cambridge University Press eBooks. https://doi.org/10.1017/cbo9781139084444 — p. 38
  - Andrew Gelman & Jennifer Hill. (2006). Data Analysis Using Regression and Multilevel/Hierarchical Models. Cambridge University Press eBooks. https://doi.org/10.1017/cbo9780511790942 — p. 222

### IV-INFER-06 — Assess joint identification with a Cragg-Donald/conditional-F statistic under multiple endogenous regressors.

**Scope:** `multiple_endogenous` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** HIGH (3 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** With more than one treatment variable needing an instrument, the paper should assess joint instrument strength with a statistic built for that case, such as Cragg-Donald or conditional (Sanderson-Windmeijer) F, rather than each first stage's own F.

**Why it matters:** Separate first-stage F statistics are not designed to show whether the instruments jointly identify the effects of all the treatments.

**Check:** Whether a paper with multiple endogenous regressors reports a joint/conditional identification statistic rather than only per-equation F statistics.

- **Pass:** A fired multiple_endogenous paper reports a Cragg-Donald and/or conditional (Sanderson-Windmeijer) first-stage statistic.
- **Flag:** A multiple_endogenous paper judges strength only from separate per-equation first-stage F statistics.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Eleanor Sanderson & Frank Windmeijer. (2015). A weak instrument <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" altimg="si3.gif" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mml:mi>F</mml:mi></mml:math>-test in linear IV models with multiple endogenous variables. Journal of Econometrics, 190(2), 212-221. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeconom.2015.06.004 — pp. 212, 215
  - James H. Stock, Jonathan H. Wright, & Motohiro Yogo. (2002). A Survey of Weak Instruments and Weak Identification in Generalized Method of Moments. Journal of Business and Economic Statistics, 20(4), 518-529. https://doi.org/10.1198/073500102288618658 — p. 522
